AGENT ACCELERATION · PART 1 · 01
Agent acceleration · Part 1 of 2

Where the time and the money go

Why LLM agents that operate software are slow and expensive, and how the two are linked.

Every number comes from a published measurement of a computer-use, web or coding agent, or from a vendor’s own price page (2024–2026); the conditions of each measurement are stated next to it, and the full references are at the end of the part.

September 2026

The loop every agent runs — Part 1 puts a number on each term
read: the prompt is processed all at once · write: the answer comes out one token at a time · N passes, c model calls per pass
封面。这一部分对应文档《Agent 慢和贵的逻辑链》。讲法：先把循环讲清（第 2 页），再把慢的五类、贵的六类各给一页总览加几页代表性例子，最后讲两者怎么连、修什么能省什么、还有什么没人测过。所有文献细节表放在附录 A1–A6。
AGENT ACCELERATION · PART 1 · 02

The loop, with every term on it

here: the loop, its two equations, and the one term that grows fastest → to: the five sources of slowness

One task = one loop run times. Each pass observes the screen, makes at least one model call, acts, and waits. A call has three segments: queueing; reading the prompt, all tokens at once; writing the answer, one token at a time — 81.7 tokens per second for Claude Opus 5.5 (Artificial Analysis, 2026) — at 5× the read price. Observation, action, waiting and queueing enter only the time equation; read and write tokens enter both.

time
money
passes · model calls in pass · tokens read and written · prices (a cached read costs 0.1×) · environment time. The harness — the program around the model — sets , the observation size and the sleeps.
tokens read, cumulative tokens written, cumulative
Cumulative tokens over a task, in units of “tokens added per pass”; full history re-sent, no cache (calc.).
READING GROWS WITH THE SQUARE OF THE PASSES
10 passes re-read 55 units of history, 20 passes 210 (calc.)
Pass re-sends the earlier screenshots (1,000–1,800 tokens each; Anthropic, 2026a): doubling the passes quadruples the reading and only doubles the writing. Caching cuts the read price to 0.1× but not the shape. Measured: cost “grows quadratically with the number of steps”, later steps up to 3× slower (Abhyankar, Qi & Zhang, 2026).
SOURCES · Artificial Analysis, 2026 (third-party measurement) · Anthropic, 2026b; OpenAI, 2026 (prices) · Anthropic, 2026a · Abhyankar, Qi & Zhang, 2026

AGENT ACCELERATION · PART 1 · 03

Slowness has five sources

from the time equation → here: every cause of slowness, in five classes → to: the numbers behind each class

Four of the five are terms of the time equation; the fifth is the structure that adds them up. Which class dominates depends on the harness, not on the kind of agent (page 6). Cause-by-cause tables with measurement conditions: Appendix A1.

I · passes
II · calls per pass
III · each call
IV · environment
all added, never overlapped
V · serial
I · TOO MANY PASSES
318 tool calls per task
OSWorld 2.0, 108 hour-scale desktop tasks, Claude Opus 4.7, one action per step.
(XLANG Lab, 2026)
II · TOO MANY CALLS PER PASS
4–12 planning calls per judging call
GTA1 harness: plan, retry, judge. Sampling candidates multiplies the calls again.
(Abhyankar, Qi & Zhang, 2026)
III · EACH CALL IS SLOW
queue up to 69× · read up to 3× slower by the late passes · write 91–98.6% of model time
Identical requests by time of day; screenshots accumulate in the prompt; token-by-token writing.
(Bian et al., 2025; Abhyankar, Qi & Zhang, 2026; Yuan et al., 2026)
IV · THE ENVIRONMENT IS SLOW
3–26 s per observation · 6.6 s per browser action · 2–3 s sleep per action
Accessibility tree, browser execution, fixed sleeps; tool runs: 4% of calls take 85% of tool time.
(Abhyankar, Qi & Zhang, 2026; Wong et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2026)
V · EVERYTHING IS SERIAL
concurrency within a turn: 1.15
Nothing overlaps: task time is the sum of the classes above, so fixing one term saves only its share.
(Liu et al., 2026)

AGENT ACCELERATION · PART 1 · 04

I–II · Too many passes, too many calls per pass

from the five classes → here: the two multipliers, passes and calls per pass → to: what happens inside a call and around it

{tex("N", 15)} multiplies everything and {tex("c_k", 15)} multiplies {tex("N", 15)}. Passes pile up because tasks are long, each pass does one action, navigation-only passes still go through the model, and the agent idles or loops; calls pile up because the harness plans, judges and reflects, or samples several candidates per step.

I-1, I-2 · LONG TASKS, ONE ACTION PER PASS
318 tool calls per task
OSWorld 2.0, 108 long tasks, Claude Opus 4.7, one action per step. Several actions per call: 160.7 for the same model, 103 for Claude Opus 4.8.
(XLANG Lab, 2026)
I-3 · NAVIGATION-ONLY PASSES
66.7% of steps are pure navigation
Median of 151 WebVoyager tasks on live websites; three text agents driven by GPT-4o.
(Wong et al., 2026)
I-4 · IDLING AND DEAD LOOPS
66% of steps wasted · one loop: 27 min, $8.47
GTA1 harness on 39 OSWorld tasks: failed tasks past 50 steps; one element-locating loop repeated a step 18 times, at list price without caching.
(Abhyankar, Qi & Zhang, 2026)
II · PLAN + JUDGE + REFLECT, OR SAMPLE
4–12 planning calls per judging call · 9.6× tokens for 4.4 points
GTA1: four parallel planners, up to three retries, one judge. Sampling 1 → 10 candidates per step: 38.8% → 43.2% success, 96K → 920K tokens (gpt-oss-120b, 165 WebArena-Lite tasks). GitHub Copilot: 6.6 model calls per user turn.
(Abhyankar, Qi & Zhang, 2026; Lee et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026)

AGENT ACCELERATION · PART 1 · 05

III–V · Inside a call, around it, and in sequence

from the multipliers → here: the per-call and per-pass terms → to: which term dominates

Inside a call: queueing, reading, writing. Around it: observation, execution, fixed sleeps, tool runs. All of it runs strictly in sequence, so task time is the sum, not the largest term.

III-1, III-2 · QUEUEING AND READING
up to 69× by time of day · up to 3× slower by the late passes · 7.14× when the cache is evicted
15 models at 5 providers; the prompt at pass carries screenshots; a richer observation multiplied the input 4.8×; GLM-4.6 on 8 H100s under load.
(Bian et al., 2025; Abhyankar, Qi & Zhang, 2026; Chang et al., 2026; Kang et al., 2026)
III-3, III-4 · WRITING AND THINKING
91–98.6% of model time · 224K vs 37K output tokens per task
Warm cache, local 27–31B models; Claude Opus 4.8 vs GPT-5.5 on the same 108 tasks. More reasoning effort lowered accuracy in 21 of 36 pairs (21,730 runs).
(Yuan et al., 2026; XLANG Lab, 2026; Kapoor et al., 2025)
IV · THE ENVIRONMENT
3–26 s per accessibility tree · 6.6 s browser vs 4.7 s model per step · 2–3 s sleep per action
OSWorld desktop apps; 151 WebVoyager live-site tasks (GPT-4o); OSWorld 2.0’s sleep × 318 steps ≈ 16 min (calc.). Coding: 4% of tool calls take 85% of tool time.
(Abhyankar, Qi & Zhang, 2026; Wong et al., 2026; xlang-ai, 2026; XLANG Lab, 2026; Zhu et al., 2026)
V · SERIAL
concurrency within a turn: 1.15
GitHub Copilot telemetry. Fixing one term saves only its own share. Strip the human first: 80–92% of a coding session’s elapsed time is the person thinking.
(Liu et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2026)

AGENT ACCELERATION · PART 1 · 06

Which term dominates depends on the harness, not on the kind of agent

from the five classes → here: the shares, per kind of agent → to: the six sources of cost

All five classes exist in every agent; the heaviest term differs, and it flips when the harness changes. The one multiplier common to all three kinds is the number of passes, {tex("N", 15)}.

Screenshot desktop agent, multi-call harnessText web agentCoding agent with a prompt cache
heaviest Reading × calls per pass × passes. 87–97% of task time in planning, judging and reflection calls; screenshots and actions under 3.5% together (GTA1, Agent S2; 39 OSWorld tasks) (Abhyankar, Qi & Zhang, 2026) Browser execution and waiting. Per step, median: browser 6.6 s, model 4.7 s (151 WebVoyager live-site tasks, GPT-4o) (Wong et al., 2026) Writing, or tool tails. Writing is 91–98.6% of model time (Yuan et al., 2026); Claude Code / Codex requests: tools 59.8%, model 41.0% (Zhu et al., 2026); Copilot: model 13.7%, tools 2% (Liu et al., 2026)
flips when The harness makes one call per pass: over 70% of the time is then the sandbox, because the benchmark sleeps 2–3 s after every action (Chang et al., 2026; xlang-ai, 2026; XLANG Lab, 2026) The observation grows: 4.8× input moved the model’s share from 46.9% to 61.6% (Chang et al., 2026); the Browser-Use harness spends 73% of its latency in model calls (Winston et al., 2026) Load evicts the cache: latency up to 7.14× (Kang et al., 2026); or the tools are light and the model dominates again (Copilot)
in one line Slow in reading: every pass re-reads the growing screenshot history Slow in the environment — until the observation grows, then slow in reading Reading is cached away; slow in writing and in the tools
1 · The harness sets the dominant term — calls per pass, observation size, fixed sleeps, cache on or off. “Agents are slow because inference is slow” holds only for multi-call screenshot agents.
2 · multiplies every term — one pass fewer saves a whole pass of time and money in all three kinds; OSWorld 2.0’s authors list “fewer environment rounds” as a goal in its own right.

AGENT ACCELERATION · PART 1 · 07

Cost has six sources

from where the time goes → here: every cause of cost, in six classes → to: four ways of counting, and the machines

Money comes from two things only — tokens read and tokens written, each times a price. Writing costs 5× reading; a cached read costs 0.1×; fast mode costs 2× (Anthropic, 2026b; OpenAI, 2026). Three of the other sources multiply those two tokens; the last is the one nobody counts.

3 · number of calls
1 · tokens read
2 · tokens written
5 · unit price
4 · failures, retries
+ machine hours
6 · the machines
1 · TOKENS READ
quadratic in the passes
1,000–1,800 tokens per screenshot; rich observations 4.8×; sampling 96K → 920K; even at a 95.7% cache hit rate, prefix tokens are 59.5% of the bill.
(Abhyankar, Qi & Zhang, 2026; Anthropic, 2026a; Chang et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2026)
2 · TOKENS WRITTEN
5× the price, billed while thinking — yet 31% of an uncached bill
224K vs 37K output tokens per task (Claude Opus 4.8 vs GPT-5.5); GTA1 on 39 OSWorld tasks: $2.43 output only, $7.87 all tokens.
(XLANG Lab, 2026; Abhyankar, Qi & Zhang, 2026)
3 · NUMBER OF CALLS
multiplies both bills
5–13× the calls of a single-call harness per step (GTA1, calc.); sampling multiplies by the candidate count.
(Abhyankar, Qi & Zhang, 2026; Lee et al., 2026)
4 · FAILURES AND RETRIES
$72.4 per attempt → ≈ $351 per success
OSWorld 2.0’s best agent completes 20.6% (calc.; an accounting conversion). A dead loop bills $8.47; one leaderboard run cost ≈ $40,000.
(XLANG Lab, 2026; Abhyankar, Qi & Zhang, 2026; Kapoor et al., 2025)
5 · UNIT PRICE
$4 / $20 vs $0.10 / $0.50 per million tokens
Claude Opus 5.5 vs GPT-6 Luna, read / write; fast mode 2× and it drops the cache; cache write 1.25×, read 0.1×; above 272K tokens 2× (OpenAI).
(Anthropic, 2026b; OpenAI, 2026)
6 · THE MACHINES
0.3–4.6% of a $7.87 bill for a one-hour CPU environment (calc.)
No benchmark reports machine dollars — every “cost per task” is an API bill; from hourly list prices, $0.02–0.36 per hour (next page).
vendor price pages, read 2026-09-27

AGENT ACCELERATION · PART 1 · 08

Counting the same task four ways, and the machines nobody counts

from the six classes → here: which convention a cost figure uses, and what the environment adds → to: how slow and expensive are linked

“What does one task cost?” has four honest answers up to 30× apart, and none of them includes the machine. The first question back is always: under which convention?

conventionthe same run, counted both waysgap
output only vs all tokensGTA1 on 39 OSWorld tasks, o3 list price, no cache: $2.43 counting output only; $7.87 counting all tokens (Abhyankar, Qi & Zhang, 2026)3.2×
per attempt vs per successOSWorld 2.0, Claude Opus 4.8: $72.4 per attempt at 20.6% completion → ≈ $351 (calc.; not the cost of retrying to success) (XLANG Lab, 2026)4.9×
uncached vs cachedA cached read costs 0.1×; but at a 95.7% hit rate, prefix tokens were still 59.5% of the bill (4,265 Claude Code / Codex sessions) (Anthropic, 2026b; Zhu et al., 2026)10× read price only
standard vs fast modeClaude Opus 5.5 $4 / $20 → $8 / $40; OpenAI 2× on every listed model; up to 2.5× faster writing (vendor-stated), reading unchanged (Anthropic, 2026b; OpenAI, 2026)2×
The three that apply to a whole bill compound to about 31× (3.2 × 4.9 × 2, calc.). Screenshot-agent measurements do not report their cache state.
6 · THE MACHINES, FROM LIST PRICES
a one-hour CPU environment: $0.02–0.36 → 0.3–4.6% of a $7.87 bill, 0.03–0.5% of $72.4 (calc.)
Benchmarks name their instances but never their cost; products (Meta Muse, ChatGPT agent) run a dedicated cloud machine per user and publish no price. It grows large with plan fees, residential-proxy traffic ($5–12 per GB), wall-clock billing while the agent waits (the median AgentSysBench session is active 20% of its lifetime), and GPU sandboxes (an H100 at $3.95 per hour is half of a $7.87 bill).
vendor price pages, read 2026-09-27; Chang et al., 2026; Meta, 2026

AGENT ACCELERATION · PART 1 · 09

How slow and expensive are linked: three kinds of relationship

from the two bills → here: what each cause does to time and to money → to: the levers

The two equations share the read and write tokens; environment time and queueing appear only in the time equation. So every cause relates to time and money in exactly one of three ways.

time
money
in both equations — same sourcetime equation only — slow but not expensivethe price — money for time or accuracy
SAME SOURCE — in both equations
fix it, and time and money fall together
Passes (time ≈ linear, read tokens quadratic), calls per pass , reading, writing (the slowest and dearest token), cache hits (fragile: editing the history or switching to fast mode invalidates them), failures and idle loops (which also turn “per attempt” into “per success”).
(Abhyankar, Qi & Zhang, 2026; Anthropic, 2026b)
SLOW BUT NOT EXPENSIVE — time equation only
fix it, and only time falls
Queueing, page loads and fixed sleeps, tool tails. None produces a token; the machine behind them is billed by the hour, usually under 5% of the API bill. Escaping the queue means a fast or priority tier — at 2× the price.
MONEY FOR TIME OR FOR ACCURACY — opposite signs
buying speed buys only the writing segment
Fast mode: up to 2.5× faster writing (vendor-stated), reading unchanged, 2× the price. Bigger models, more thinking: cost versus accuracy is convex — each extra point costs more than the last (marginal tokens per point 101K → 575K; 6×, 9×, 9.6× the tokens for a few points), and more thinking is not always more accurate.
(Anthropic, 2026b; OpenAI, 2026; XLANG Lab, 2026; Kapoor et al., 2025; Lee et al., 2026)
In one line: a cause that lives in tokens — fix it and time and money fall together; a cause that lives in waiting — fix it and only time falls; paying for speed buys only the writing segment.
SOURCES · Abhyankar, Qi & Zhang, 2026 · Anthropic, 2026b · OpenAI, 2026 · XLANG Lab, 2026 · Kapoor et al., 2025 · Lee et al., 2026 — the cause-by-cause table is Appendix A5

AGENT ACCELERATION · PART 1 · 10

The levers, and what is still unmeasured

from the three relationships → here: what fixing each lever buys, and the holes in the evidence → to: Part 2, what the literature has done with each lever

Seven levers follow from the equations; each saves a known term and carries a known risk. Part 2 asks how far the literature has pushed each one. On the right: what no measurement has settled — gaps in the evidence, not claims of a research gap.

levertimemoneythe catch
Fewer passes — several actions per call, skip navigation-only stepsyesyes, the quadratic termwhich steps need no thinking?
Read less — trim history, shrink screenshots, cache the prefixyesyesforgets; trimming invalidates the cache
Write less — less thinking, smaller modelyesyesaccuracy may fall
Fewer calls per pass — drop judging and reflectionyesyesfewer errors caught
Overlap the waiting — pre-load, parallel tools, page-ready eventsyesnoonly where the environment dominates
Buy a fast or priority tierwriting onlyno — 2× morereading unchanged; cache dropped
Stop retrying failures — early stop, detect dead loopsyesyeskills some attempts that would succeed
NOT YET MEASURED
  • Read / write time split and cache hit rate for a frontier API model — the only split is on local 27–31B models (Yuan et al., 2026); screenshot-agent measurements do not report cache state.
  • How much slower than a person — no benchmark times agent and human on the same tasks; the closest, AXIS’s small user study, has a UI agent 1.69× slower than manual work on easy tasks (Lu et al., 2025).
  • Whether the benchmark’s fixed sleep sits inside “action” time in OSWorld-Human — if so, “environment under 3.5%” understates the waiting.
  • How much slowness costs accuracy — OSWorld 2.0 records the stale-screen failure mode without its share (XLANG Lab, 2026); the rebound from a smaller model has no direct evidence.
SOURCES · levers derived from the two equations on page 2 · gaps: Yuan et al., 2026 · Lu et al., 2025 · XLANG Lab, 2026 · Appendix A5 and A6

AGENT ACCELERATION · PART 1 · A1 · 1/3

A1 · Slowness, every cause — I. steps and II. calls per step

the complete table behind pages 3–4 · three kinds of agent: screenshot desktop agent, text web agent, coding agent with a prompt cache
idcausemechanismevidence, with the conditions of the measurementsourcedominant in
I-1The task is longHour-scale tasks take hundreds of passesOSWorld 2.0, 108 long tasks: Claude Opus 4.7 with maximum thinking, one action per step, 500-step cap: 318 tool calls per task on average, i.e. 318 steps; with several actions per call, Claude Opus 4.8 takes 103 steps (481.8 calls) and GPT-5.5 95.2 steps (149.8 calls)(XLANG Lab, 2026)screenshot, text
I-2One action per passEvery click is a whole pass: one observation, one model call, one waitOSWorld 2.0: with one action per step Claude Opus 4.7 needs 318 steps; with batched actions the same model needs 160.7 and Claude Opus 4.8 needs 103(XLANG Lab, 2026)screenshot, text
I-3Navigation-only passes still call the modelPaging, scrolling and opening the next page need no thinking but cost a call eachSkim’s profile of three text web agents (Browser-Use, AgentOccam, WebVoyager; GPT-4o) on 151 WebVoyager live-site tasks: 66.7% of the steps in the median task are pure navigation(Wong et al., 2026)text
I-4Idling and dead loopsElement not found, repeated retries; steps rise without progressOSWorld-Human’s records of the GTA1 harness (o3 plans and judges, GTA1-7B locates elements) on 39 OSWorld desktop tasks: in failed tasks that exceeded 50 steps, 66% of steps were wasted repeats; one element-locating loop repeated the same step 18 times — 27 minutes and $8.47 at list price without caching(Abhyankar, Qi & Zhang, 2026)screenshot
I-5Acting on a stale screenThe screenshot is taken before the page changes; the agent clicks on the old layout and must repairOSWorld 2.0 records “stale interface state” as a failure mode; no share reported(XLANG Lab, 2026)screenshot
II-1Multi-call harnessOne step = plan + judge + reflect, several calls in seriesOSWorld-Human, two harnesses: GTA1 runs 4 parallel planners per step, retries up to 3 rounds, then one judging call picks — 4–12 planning calls per judging call; Agent S2 adds a reflection call per step, so planning is 53% and reflection 34% of task time(Abhyankar, Qi & Zhang, 2026)screenshot
II-2Sampling for accuracy5–20 candidates per step, then pick oneSame model and harness (gpt-oss-120b, ReAct) on 165 WebArena-Lite tasks: 1 → 10 candidates per step raises success from 38.8% to 43.2% and tokens per task from 96K to 920K — 9.6× the tokens for 4.4 points(Lee et al., 2026)text
II-3Coding agents call repeatedly within a turnThe model is called back and forth inside one user turnGitHub Copilot coding agent production telemetry (first week of June 2026, 13.5 million sessions): 6.6 model calls per user turn on average(Liu et al., 2026)coding

A1 · Slowness, every cause — III. each call is slow

the complete table behind page 5
idcausemechanismevidence, with the conditions of the measurementsourcedominant in
III-1QueueingThe request waits at the provider; unbilled, but counted as model timeClient-side measurement of 15 models across 5 providers: requests of the same length differ in latency by up to 69× depending on when they are sent(Bian et al., 2025)all
III-2Reading (the prompt is re-processed every call)Every call re-reads the whole history; more screenshots, slowerOSWorld-Human, multi-call harnesses: later steps up to 3× slower because the prompt at step k holds the k−1 earlier screenshots — “dominated by prefill”. One screenshot is 1,000–1,800 tokens. AgentSysBench’s WebArena agent (Kimi-K2.6): observation switched from a single format to accessibility tree + HTML + screenshot → input 4.8×, model share of time 46.9% → 61.6%. Under load the cache is evicted and re-read: SWE-Agent / OpenHands running GLM-4.6 on 8 H100s for SWE-bench Lite, request latency up to 7.14× as concurrency rises(Abhyankar, Qi & Zhang, 2026; Anthropic, 2026a; Chang et al., 2026; Kang et al., 2026)screenshot; text with rich observations; coding under load
III-3Writing (one token at a time)Token-by-token generation, strictly serialLocally served ReAct agents (Qwen3.6-27B / Gemma4-31B, vLLM, 2 H100s) on five benchmarks: with the cache warm, generation is 91–98.6% of model time. Windows desktop agent UFO2 (GPT-4o / o1 API): about 10 s per model call, the largest item per step in every configuration(Yuan et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2025)coding; single-call screenshot
III-4Thinking modes and larger modelsThinking writes more tokens; larger models are slower per tokenOSWorld 2.0, same 108 tasks: Claude Opus 4.8 writes 224K output tokens per task, GPT-5.5 37K. Holistic Agent Leaderboard, 9 benchmarks, 21,730 runs: raising reasoning effort lowered accuracy in 21 of 36 pairs(XLANG Lab, 2026; Kapoor et al., 2025)all

A1 · Slowness, every cause — IV. environment, V. serial

the complete table behind page 5 (environment and serial structure)
idcausemechanismevidence, with the conditions of the measurementsourcedominant in
IV-1Producing the observationExtracting the accessibility tree or detecting elements takes timeOSWorld desktop applications: 3–26 s to generate one accessibility tree; the screenshot itself is under 2% of task time. UFO2: OmniParser element detection adds about 1 s per step(Abhyankar, Qi & Zhang, 2026; Zhang et al., 2025)screenshot
IV-2Browser execution and page loadAfter a click the agent waits for the page151 WebVoyager live-site tasks: per step, median browser action 6.6 s vs model call 4.7 s. WebArena with GenericAgent + Claude 3.5 Sonnet: 7.6 s of a 12.2 s step in the browser (this figure was not re-verified)(Wong et al., 2026; Le Sellier De Chezelles et al., 2025)text
IV-3Fixed sleepsThe agent cannot tell when the page is ready, so it sleeps a fixed number of secondsOSWorld’s environment code sleeps 2 s after every action; OSWorld 2.0 prescribes 3 s, so 318 steps are about 16 minutes of pure waiting (calc.). AgentSysBench: a single-call GUI agent (ReAct, Kimi-K2.6 API) spends over 70% of its OSWorld execution time in the desktop sandbox(xlang-ai, 2026; XLANG Lab, 2026; Chang et al., 2026)screenshot (caused by the benchmark harness)
IV-4Tool tailsTests and builds take minutesTraceLab, 4,265 Claude Code / Codex sessions from 43 developers (September 2025 – June 2026): tool calls over 1 minute are 4% of calls but 85% of tool time; a request averages 4.3 minutes — tools 2.5 (59.8%), model 1.7 (41.0%)(Zhu et al., 2026)coding
VSerial structureThe four stages never overlap, so task time is the sum of every term, not the largest one; fixing one term saves only its shareConcurrency within a turn is 1.15 in Copilot telemetry. Separately, 80–92% of a coding session’s elapsed time is the human thinking between turns — strip it before reading any total(Liu et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2026)all

AGENT ACCELERATION · PART 1 · A2

A2 · Where the arrows land, with every measurement condition

the complete table behind page 6
screenshot desktop agent, multi-call harnesstext web agentcoding agent with a prompt cache
heaviest termReading × calls per step × steps. OSWorld-Human timed two multi-call harnesses (GTA1, Agent S2) step by step on 39 OSWorld desktop tasks: 87–97% of task time in planning, judging and reflection calls; screenshots and actions together under 3.5% (Abhyankar, Qi & Zhang, 2026)Browser execution plus waiting. Skim measured three text web agents (GPT-4o) on 151 WebVoyager live-site tasks: per step, median browser action 6.6 s and model call 4.7 s (Wong et al., 2026)Writing, or tool tails, depending on the tools. With the context cache on, token-by-token generation is 91–98.6% of model time (locally served models) (Yuan et al., 2026); in Claude Code / Codex records a request spends 59.8% in tools and 41.0% in the model (Zhu et al., 2026); in GitHub Copilot, whose tools are light, agent time is 13.7% model and 2% tools (Liu et al., 2026)
secondWriting: with thinking on, more reasoning tokens per step, and generation is one token at a timeReading, once the observation grows: AgentSysBench switched a WebArena agent from one observation format to accessibility tree + HTML + screenshot — input 4.8×, model share 46.9% → 61.6% (Chang et al., 2026); the Browser-Use harness spends 73% of its latency in model calls (Winston et al., 2026)Reading, when load evicts the cache and the whole context is re-read: ThunderAgent measured request latency up to 7.14× under cache thrash (Kang et al., 2026)
negligibleProducing the observation and executing the action: under 3.5% together (Abhyankar, Qi & Zhang, 2026)Nothing: model and browser are close; which is larger depends on observation size and model speedNavigation-only steps: a coding agent has no pages to turn
counter-exampleA single-call agent is different: AgentSysBench’s one-call GUI agent (Kimi-K2.6) spends over 70% of its OSWorld time in the desktop sandbox (Chang et al., 2026), because the harness sleeps after every action — 2 s in OSWorld’s code (xlang-ai, 2026), 3 s in OSWorld 2.0 (XLANG Lab, 2026)Browser-Use: 73% of latency in model calls, not the browser (Winston et al., 2026)Two production records point opposite ways: heavy tools in Claude Code / Codex (tools 59.8% > model 41.0%) (Zhu et al., 2026); light tools in Copilot (model 13.7% > tools 2%) (Liu et al., 2026). The difference is the kind of tool (tests and builds vs file reads), not a contradiction
in one lineSlow in reading: every step re-reads the screenshot history, more as the task goes onSlow in the environment (browser and page waits); once the observation grows, slow in reading againReading is cached away; slow in writing and in the tools

the complete table behind page 7 · prices are list prices from the vendors’ own pages, September 2026
idcausemechanismevidence, with the conditions of the measurementsource

A3 · Cost, every cause — 3. calls, 4. failures, 5. unit price

the complete table behind page 7 (calls, failures, unit price)
idcausemechanismevidence, with the conditions of the measurementsource
3Number of calls scales both token billsGTA1: 4 parallel planners per step, up to 3 retry rounds, one judging call → 4–12 planning calls per judging call, i.e. 5–13× the calls of a single-call harness (calc.). Agentic test-time scaling: 5–20 candidates per step multiply the calls by the candidate count. The same extra calls cost time and money at once(Abhyankar, Qi & Zhang, 2026; Lee et al., 2026)
4-1Failed attempts are billedCost per success = cost per attempt ÷ success rateOSWorld 2.0: the best agent (Claude Opus 4.8) costs about $72.4 per attempt at 20.6% completion → about $351 per success (calc.). An accounting conversion, not the real price of retrying one task until it succeeds(XLANG Lab, 2026)
4-2Idle steps are billed in fullEvery pass of a dead loop is a full read and writeOSWorld-Human, GTA1 on 39 OSWorld tasks: one element-locating loop repeated the same step 18 times — 27 minutes, $8.47 at list price without caching; in failed tasks over 50 steps, 66% of steps were such repeats(Abhyankar, Qi & Zhang, 2026)
4-3Evaluation itself is too expensive to repeatSingle runs, no repeatsHolistic Agent Leaderboard: 9 benchmarks, 21,730 runs, one run per configuration, about $40,000 in total; Claude Opus 4.1 not run on Online-Mind2Web because the estimate was $20,000(Kapoor et al., 2025)
5-1Model tierClaude Opus 5.5 $4 / $20 vs GPT-6 Luna $0.10 / $0.50 per million tokens read / writtenVendor price pages, 27 September 2026(Anthropic, 2026b; OpenAI, 2026)
5-2Fast mode2× on both vendors; switching speed tiers invalidates the cacheAnthropic: Claude Opus 5.5 $8 / $40, up to 2.5× output speed (vendor-stated), first-token wait unchanged. OpenAI: 2× on all listed models; “up to 2.5×” stated only for GPT-5.6 Sol(Anthropic, 2026b; OpenAI, 2026)
5-3Cache write and readWriting to the cache 1.25×; reading from it 0.1×Vendor price pages(Anthropic, 2026b; OpenAI, 2026)
5-4Long-context surchargeOpenAI: 2× the read price above 272K tokensVendor price page(OpenAI, 2026)

The four accounting conventions (page 8), in one line each: output only vs all tokens — 3.2× (OSWorld-Human, $2.43 vs $7.87); per attempt vs per success — 4.9× (OSWorld 2.0, $72.4 ÷ 20.6%); uncached vs cached — 10× on the read price, far less on the bill (TraceLab: 95.7% hits, prefix still 59.5% of cost); standard vs fast mode — 2× (both vendors), buying only writing speed.

A5 · Each cause’s effect on time and on money

the complete table behind pages 9–10
causeeffect on timeeffect on moneyrelationship
Many passes Roughly linear: one more step is one more call and one more wait (later steps somewhat slower, up to 3×)Write tokens linear in ; read tokens quadratic, because every step re-reads the whole historysame source — double the steps: about 2× the time, about 4× the read bill (uncached)
Many calls per pass linearlinearsame source
Reading a lot (history, screenshots, rich observations)Reading time, longer every stepRead-token billsame source — the same tokens cost time and money
Writing a lot (thinking)Generation time, roughly 12 ms per tokenWrite-token bill at 5× the read pricesame source, and the dearest time: writing is the slowest and the most expensive token
Cache hitsSaves reading timeRead price 0.1×same source, but fragile: editing the history or switching to fast mode invalidates it
Queueingslowfreeslow but not expensive; escaping it means a fast or priority tier at 2×
Environment waits (page loads, fixed sleeps)slowNo API cost; machine time by the hour — CPU sandboxes $0.02–0.36 per hour, usually under 5% of the API billslow but not expensive
Tool tails (tests, builds)slowNo API costslow but not expensive
Failures, idling, retriesslowexpensivesame source, and it turns “per attempt” into “per success”
Fast modeWriting up to 2.5× faster (vendor-stated); reading unchanged2× the pricemoney for time
Bigger models, more thinkingslowerdearermoney and time for accuracy, convex: marginal tokens per point 101K → 575K on one model; 6× / 9× / 9.6× tokens for a few points; more thinking not always more accurate
Smaller modelsfastercheaperbut if accuracy falls, steps and retries rise — possibly slower and dearer again (inference, no direct evidence)

AGENT ACCELERATION · PART 1 · A6

A6 · The gaps in the evidence, and what each one blocks

the complete table behind page 10
gapwhat exists todayconsequence for what can be claimed
Read / write time split and cache hit rate for a frontier API modelNo measurement reports both; the only read / write split is on locally served 27–31B models (Yuan et al., 2026); screenshot-agent measurements do not report cache stateHow much of “87–97% in the model” is reading, how much writing, and what remains once the cache is on — unknown
How much slower an agent is than a personNone of 17 benchmarks measures agent and human elapsed time on the same tasks; the closest is AXIS’s user study, in which a UI agent was 1.69× slower than manual work on easy tasks (small sample) (Lu et al., 2025)“X times slower than a person” cannot go on a slide
Environment dollarsBenchmarks report instance types; AgentSysBench reports shares; products publish nothing. Computable from instance type × duration × list price: CPU environments usually 0.3–5% of the API bill (page 8)Every benchmark cost is an API bill; the omission is small for CPU environments, not for GPU sandboxes or long idle sessions
Whether OSWorld-Human’s “action” includes the 2-s sleep after each stepNot stated (xlang-ai, 2026); if it does, “actions under 2%” implies more than 100 s per step (calc.)“Environment under 3.5%” may understate the waiting
The rebound from a smaller modelNo direct evidence on how many extra steps and retries a drop in accuracy causesThe last row of the relationship table stays marked “inference”
